editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: It's March 1st, 2005. This is an interview for the Veterans History Project. I'm talking to Mr. William H. Clegg, of 2647 Barrington, Toledo, Ohio 43606. Telephone: 419-535-7060. Mr. Clegg served in the U.S. Navy in World War II and during the Korean War. Mr. Clegg, let's begin with where you were born and we'll move from there to schools through your active service, your reserve service. You have quite a career in the Navy so we want to get all of this in.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And you were --

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I was born in Toledo, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Where did you go to school?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I went to Blessed Sacrament here in Toledo and then I entered DeVilbiss High School in the class of 1943 however during World War II when the university was operated by the city of Toledo there was an accelerated program in which seniors could enter the university in the middle of their senior year of high school which I did. So, I attended starting in January of '43 so that when I graduated from high school I had one full semester of college. I attended that following summer so when my class entered college I was a sophomore. When I was still 17 I took a civil service examination from Congressman Homer Rainey from Toledo and I was quick enough to earn an appointment to the Naval Academy when I entered and back in those days all the military schools had three year programs. At the end of my first year at the Naval Academy our class was split. The upper half graduated in three years and the lower class graduated in four years. I was fortunate enough to to follow these groups and because of my experience at the university, I was in the upper class and I graduated in June of 1947.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Let's talk a little bit about the Naval Academy?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Appointments to the Naval Academy are difficult.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: They are.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: They're right around all 50 states so to get in this was quite an honor?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, it was quite a selective process, I admit.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And also I understand that the Naval Academy like West Point is a tough grind maybe in your first year?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes, it was. The attrition was fairly high in the first year and there were certain courses such as organic chemistry and and descriptive geometry which were kind of the determining factors which if you couldn't pass those you'd never succeed, so most of the dropouts and the people who failed were during the first year.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Were the instructors or the pleb classmen or whatever they were called, were they as tough as we have seen in the movies?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, in my era we used to say we had the last real pleb year with the hazing and there was a method to this. It certainly taught you discipline, it taught you to preen your memory because you were asked all kinds of questions and if you didn't supply the proper answer there was what we call the come around, you'd go around to the first classman room and at the study hour and sometimes you were subjected to physical torment but we all lived through it. It was part of growing up.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Is that something that would be acceptable today?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: That's right, there's no more hazing which is good in itself but it should be replaced by more leeze training I think.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Which is even better.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, you graduated in three years?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Again with honors.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, half of my class graduated four years, I was fortunate enough to graduate in three. At the end of the three years my class standing was 144 out of the original 1100. Approximately 500 graduated in three years and half of them, about 500 graduated in four years.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: What was your rank then?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I was an ensign in the U.S. Navy. My first assignment was to the USS Missouri Battleship, BB-63. There were four of them in that class at the time and my first real cruise was to Rio de Janeiro in September of 1947. I had been on the ship for about two months.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: What was your assignment?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I was assistant navigator and it was a little unusual in that Harry Truman, then president decided to attend the Rio de Janeiro Conference in September of 1947 but he wanted to visit his ship he called it. His daughter christened the Missouri so he figured that was his ship because he was from Missouri so we sailed to Rio de Janeiro and we made several stops to several islands in the Caribbean along the way and contrary to usual tradition when you cross the equator for the first time, you're endoctrinated into a shellback ceremony. We decided, the captain decided to delay that so that Harry Truman could participate on his trip coming back north. So, we sailed to Rio, we met Harry Truman there and his official party, his wife, his daughter, Admiral Leahy, his whole staff, the news people, they were just all over the ship. Harry Truman used to take his morning walk around the deck, which was quite a walk, the ship was 888 feet long and one of my jobs as assistant navigator was to post the ship's position and of course, we'd get home taking the stars at night and the sun during the day and we'd plot our positions at 0800; 1200 and 2000, three times a day and we'd get to file those reports. So, when we get there it was my job to go down to the officer's wardroom and on a big chart post our positions, make notes on the chart and then there was a similar chart in the admiral's quarters where President Truman and his people were staying. Each time I went down to post a position I'd have to tell the sentry outside his cabin, the marine sentry who it was, so he would check to see if it was all right and I would go in and usually Harry Truman and four or five of his cronies were sitting in the corner playing poker. And Truman was a little eventful in that on our way back from Rio de Janeiro to Norfolk we came across a commercial freighter who was carrying a man who had an emergency, needed emergency surgery so we came alongside and we transferred the patient over to our ship and the ship docked and then when we crossed the equator Harry Truman and all his people were involved in this. Crossing the equator is quite a thing in the Navy and I have a certificate that says I was initiated into the Shellback Ceremony but the unusual thing I think I'm one of the few people who was a resident of North America who had the Shellback Ceremony crossing traveling north.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, President Truman was part of the hazing process?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, he went through the motion but he didn't get dunked and he didn't get greased with all of them, and the King Neptune, one of the chefs, a big fellow, was sitting there on the throne and he had grease all over his stomach and one of the things we had to do was kiss his stomach and then we were dunked in this big tub of water and went through a mild hazing thing. It wasn't tough at all. It was fun. I always wore a crew top, and if you didn't have a crew top they gave you one right there. I was always qualified for that.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: You said you were the assistant navigator there?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Was there ever a time when the navagation of the ship was entirely in your hands?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, not really because my boss who was a full commander, he was a navigator, the captain of the ship was a full captain and second officers were the commander, and the navigator who was a commander all had staterooms around the bridge, they never left the area. My stateroom was down below in the bunk room and my job was to be up before the morning stars and in the northern latitude this was quite early and I stayed up there all day. They brought our meals up there on a tray. I had to sample the food for the enlisted men, so it was the same food that they had and then I had to stay up there until after evening stars which was about 20 minutes after sunset which could have been quite late and my orders had to be written and then it was time to go to bed. So, I would work anywhere from 18 to 20 hours a day, seven days a week and I was always on the bridge when we were in sight of land to do the navigating.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Another question, when did this trip to Rio take place?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: September of 1947.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Oh, I see, from -- Any threats from an enemy had long been passed?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: No problem whatsoever.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And then you went from the Missouri back to the Naval Academy?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes, after a little over a year on the ship, I got orders to go to CIC, The Combat Information Center School in Chicago and about a week later I got another set of orders cancelling those and I was ordered to go to the Naval Academy as an instructor and this was unusual because when I was a midshipman all the instructors were lieutenants and above, some commanders, some lieutenant commanders and the superintendent at that time decided to try something new, that he was going to have senior officers who had been at sea for at least seven years, rather than have them come back as instructors he wanted to have junior officers who had some sea experience. Since I had been doing navigating for over a year I guess they decided that I would serve the Navy well by going into the Naval Academy. I was an instructor in the Navigation Department for a little over a year and then at the end of my tour which was, I knew earlier when I went in, I was ordered to a minesweeper in Japan.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: How did you get to Japan?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, I took the train from Annapolis -- no, I had a car, I drove my car to Toledo, sold the car, took the train to San Francisco, stayed there a couple days and then I'd got on a Mars Mariner, a seaplane to fly from Alameda to Hickam Field in Hawaii, stayed there a couple days and then I got on a transport plane, one of the real old, I think it was an R4D Transport which had -- didn't have any chairs or seats, it had rodes made into seats and we had all the cargo in front of us, we had box lunches, we stopped at Johnston Island for refueling and then we stopped at Kwajalein overnight. I'll never forget going into the mess hall. I was thirsty and someone said, here's the water, so I got a drink of water and I said, gee, this looks like ice tea, it's so brown, but it was water. It was good. And then we went from Kwajalein to Guam, stayed there for a couple days and then from Guam on to Tokyo.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: How long did this journey take?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, the actual flying time, I added it up later was 40 hours of actual flying time.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: On the rode seat?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, part of it was that, that was the trip to Hawaii and then the rest from Hawaii to Japan was on the rode seat, but it was not bad.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Why would you have been chosen to go from an Annapolis instructor to minesweeper duty? How does that occur?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, you never know. The detail officer was called in the Pentagon for a meeting and they tried to give officers varied assignments and I'm guessing, well, this fellow was on a battleship, what he needs is some small ship duty, and I think that's how I was assigned to a minesweeper. Very small, 136 foot wooden hull because we were sweeping mines. When I got there, there were six ships sweeping mines in the Inland Sea and between Japan and Korea. They were out, so I had to stay in Army barracks for three or four days until the ships came in over the weekend and I finally met up with my ship. I was the Third Officer. There were three officers on one of those small minesweepers, about 25 men, and my job, well, what we'd do is divide all the duties up by three and these were my duties on board the Chatterer. I was the executive officer, the operations officer, the navigator, the engineering officer, supply officer, and also athletic officer which is important because when we're in port we used to have athletic contests and I remember one of the other ships challenged us to a basketball game. Well, we only had 25 men and three officers and I was the athletic officer and I could only scare up four guys from our crew, so I became the fifth player in the basketball team and I was pretty young then and I thought I was in pretty good shape but I wasn't used to playing a full game with no substitution. That was interesting.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Why would you be sweeping mines after the war?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, there are two reasons; one, the U.S. Army/Air Force laid magnetic mines in the Inland Sea to mine the different harbors and this was 1950, no, it was the fall of '49, and the U.S. insurance companies would not insure any U.S. cargo ships going into Japanese ports unless the U.S. minesweepers had cleared the mines. So, what we did when we were sweeping magnetic mines we had two ships paired together and we had a cable joining the two and we used to travel about 50 feet apart and we'd have a long cable streaming behind us. One ship was generally haltered with a 540 kilowat generator connected to the other ship and the other ship would do the navigating. So, we would go in pairs and hopefully that cable behind us would sweep, about a six inch cable with a halter going through it, and would explode any magnetic mines that were laying on the bottom.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Why would a mine be laying on the bottom?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, it's shallow and the mines were very intricate. Some of them had timers on them; some of them had counters; some just a magnetic attraction, that's why we were using wooden ships. If a steel ship had gone through there it would set off the mines or in other cases that had a counter you never knew what the count was. They could set the counter to go off and the first time someone passed by or the second or third or the fourth or the tenth and so we had to sweep the same lanes a number of times.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: While you were in the process did you explode a lot of mines?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: No, some. Fortunately, they were far enough after. What we used to do is sweep in formation so that the other two ships they would travel inside the floats that we had showing the marker so that they wouldn't be exposed to any mines because that lane had already been swept.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, were these mines laying there in the same position when they were dropped or did they have a way of floating?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: No, they were heavy and they were just single.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: They didn't float into shore?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: No, they just stayed on the bottom.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And these were American mines or were they Japanese?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: These were American mines.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: The Japanese didn't have any mines?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: They did but I'll tell you what they did.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: We were also equipped to take care of pressure mines. Pressure from the ship would explode the mines. We had what we'd call eggcrates that we would pull that would create pressure. Now, our ships were very small. They're a wooden hull, they float high, they didn't have any metal to attract the mines. So, we were equipped for a combination of different mines. We never knew what was going to be there. The interesting thing is every time we would clear a harbor, the local Japanese would have a big party for us. I have some pictures I didn't bring down but I remember one at Himeji Castle, huge beautiful castle and when we cleared their harbor they had a big party for us. We toured the castle. It was very intricate. The guide would say, see that little thing up there, oh, yeah, well, there's an imperfection in the construction right there. I didn't notice it. He said, yeah, the architect was so embarrassed he lost face and when that was pointed out to him he stuck a chisel in his mouth and jumped off the top and killed himself because he lost face.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: That's been going on a long time. So, they would have a party for you because now they could use the, they were fishermen?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, that, and not only that but U.S. ships could come in but they were afraid for business.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: And that was in the Inland Sea and then we went over, I didn't mention but I reported to my ship we were in the Island of Kyushu, a small island, and we were sweeping in between the island and in between Japan and Korea there were some mines there and then we were ordered to go to Hokido. We traveled, we left from Kobi as I remember, that was the original capital of Japan. So, we went from Kobi up to probably the eastern coast of Japan and there's a strait between Honshu where Tokyo and Yokahama are and Hokkaido, we put in half the Adotti, there was a typhoon coming, and I must say, I'll never forget that. These were wooden ships and they would bobb like a cork, and I can remember sitting in the small ward room which was no bigger than this den and I sat there all night with my life jacket on and I would watch the tube barometer which should show the roll of the ship and I remember it going 58 degrees one way and 58 degrees the other way and a couple more degrees and we would have turned over.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Let's talk about life aboard that little ship. You spent your whole day on the ship?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Bobbing around in the sea?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yeah, and we'd go all night. Usually we'd go out Monday morning early and sweep mines until we ended the day on Thursday.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, you spent your sleeping hours on the deck also?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yeah, there were only three officers and we stood watch every four hours. Going by the ship's time from midnight till 4 was called the mid-watch and from 4 to 8, 8 to 12 and 12 to 4, 4 to 8, 8 to 12 and every eight hours you'd have another four hour watch. And then you had to do your regular job during the eight hours, you had to eat and sleep.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Were you ever seasick from that bobbing?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: No, it never did. I remember one time the weather was pretty bad and I had had a mid-watch and I came down at four o'clock in the morning and I was hungry and there were only two guys on the ship that were not seasick, one was a chief engineman who worked for me and myself. Well, the galley was a shamble because everything was all over the place. All we could find were some coldcuts and some ribs and we made sandwiches. That's the closest I ever came to being seasick, it was bad. We had one guy who was the chief bulletin mate who had been in the Navy almost 20 years and every time we went to sea the first day he was sick but he would just lie down in a corner for one or two days and after that he'd get up and he was fine. Great guy, a terrific worker. He said he got seasick every time he started out on these.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I sympathize. Well, now did you get ashore? Did you visit the Japanese cities?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes, the first time we were in Kokur and there wasn't too much there. We later went to Kobi and were based in Kobi and we did mindsweeping in the sea there. I went to Kobi and a number of other small towns and then we went to the Yafriska, which was a main base, a Navy base, and from there I remember taking the train up to Tokyo. I used to know the names of all the cities we passed through, Kamakur and Syrikamakur and a number of other ones up to Tokyo. I remember the first time I went, I forgot to tell you that my ship was in drydock in Yafriska and while the ship was in drydock I went to a naval hospital for a minor operation and that's when I met my wife on her first day of duty. It was one of those on my tailbone. I had trouble sitting down so they gave me a rubber donut. So, I took that with me on the train and I was getting along fine, the train was bouncing along and all of a sudden, whoosh, my donut blew out and I didn't have a donut for the rest of the trip, but Tokyo is an amazing place. The first time I got there, the train station at Tokyo reminded me of Grand Central Station, only much larger, and as we got out and got in the main area some Japanese policeman blew a whistle and the crowd parted like the Red Sea and this other fellow and I walked through the crowd to the other side and when we got to the other side he blew a whistle and they started milling around again.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Very interesting, why?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, we were the capturers and we were the occupation and we never had any problems but they were going through this occupation period until the occupation period was over, the Japanese were very polite and never saw any incident. The only problem I had was I went in a barber shop to get a haircut because we didn't have any barbers on those small ships and the Japanese gentleman who was with me, a young fellow, gave me a haircut using just a straight razor, and I can remember when I sat in the barber chair, I said to myself, I hope this fellow isn't a former kamikaze pilot but I didn't have any problem.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, they were generally friendly?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: They were very friendly.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And restrained?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, probably a little bit of each. They tried to be friendly and never had any problem.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: But that was the attitude of people who had been fierce fighters?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yeah, and we all heard stories of what would have happened if we hadn't dropped the A-bomb, if we had to invade, they would have fought to the death for their emperor.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: There would have been maybe a million people on each side?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yeah, maybe a million people on each side could have died.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: At least. Maybe a million each day.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, you spent how much time on the Chatterer?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Oh, about a year, about a year. After a stint at the drydock, while we were in the drydock we had such a small ship and there was such a big drydock that the Russians returned from frigates that we had lent them or leased in World War II. They returned these frigates and it was interesting that they never let their crew ashore, they brought the ship in followed by their own ship but they entered Tokyo Bay they turned off all the lubrication equipment. They brought the ships in, they anchored them, they took the people off, and they left. The frigates were in such terrible shape that they all had to go to the drydock, so one of them was in the same drydock we were. Well, we didn't have a lot of equipment in our ship, we used to trade equipment between ships, I was a supply officer, so if they were low on lube oil, I would trade it for something else who needed lines to tie up the ship so we would trade for it, but I needed some lyco (ph) and I said I'll go to the frigate in drydock so I went over there and I couldn't believe it. The ship was literally stripped. Anything that was movable was gone, including all the light bulbs. Anyway, after we got out of drydock we were ordered to go through to the LaPerouse Straits which is between Hokkaido and the Sakhalin Islands. The Russians had taken over Sakhalin Islands and they were occupying that and this is when we ran into that typhoon on the way up. We all managed to survive and we had a little wait and the northern tip of Hokkaido, there were only two ships, another ship and ours and this time we were going to do minesweeping of anchored mines. These were Japanese mines. There was only about on a 20 miles stretch between the Hokkaido and the southern tip of the Sakhalin Islands, and they put more mines were there, these were floating mines and they have anchors with chains. The anchors were on the bottom and the mines were floating somewhere between the bottom and the surface, you couldn't see them, but we knew they were there. So, we had to sweep those mines and as a matter of fact there were three ships because we used to travel in a formation, one ship and the lead, and this time we had cutters streaming out but we called it a pig that was afloat, so you could see where the last one was and we would take the lead and the other two ships would have their bows inside the float, so they were in swept waters and then they have theirs streaming out, and then we made a number of passes back and forth and the idea here was that if you contacted a chain, we had cutters, very, something like bolt cutters, only much larger. The cutters would contact the chains supporting the mines and they would cut the chain, the mine would, this is a big round one with spikes going on it, it would pop to the surface and then one of the other ships would take their 22 millimeter cannon and shoot it, explode it. And that was interesting. That was --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Let's get back to something very, very important. You met your wife, the dentist.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: You also said that she outranked you?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, how does a romance in the Navy blossom when your future wife outranks you?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, this was not unusual in World War II and Korean War. She had been in the, she was a nurse, graduated and went in the Navy and another interview which she'll tell her full story, but she was assigned to a number of hospitals in the United States and then she went to Guam. And then she was there for about a year and then she was transferred from Guam to the naval hospital in Yopiscus, and that's where I met her, on her first day of duty. About that time I found I couldn't pass the eye exam. It was felt in those days that you either had to be an aviator or submariner or maybe somewhere both if you really wanted to get promoted and I couldn't pass the eye exam so I resigned my regular Navy Commission and accepted a position in the Naval Reserve.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So this then would have been in --

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: This was the summer of 1950.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I had resigned several months earlier than that and I had orders to be released from active duty.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Where did you resign? Were you in Japan?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I was in Japan on a minesweeper.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: And I came back to the US on a ship and was discharged in Treasure Island in San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, is she still in Guam?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: She's still in Japan.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: She was there for maybe another six months or so.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: And then when she was transferred back to the United States, I had been recalled to active duty for two years and while I was stationed, I was stationed in Newport and she was stationed at the naval hospital in Quantico, Virginia and we got married in Quantico, Virginia on the Marine base. I even had to borrow a Marine sword to cut the cake. Anyway after a few months, she was able to get a transfer to Newport Naval Hospital where we both remained until I was separated in October of '53. So, we had been married over a little over a year by then.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So love conquers all?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yeah. Then I decided that if they are going to keep calling me back, I should remain active. So, I joined the Naval Reserve unit in New Jersey and I was there until 1960 when we were transferred to Toledo. I had been with Ohio for about a year.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Let's go back to Japan?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: You're on a little minesweeper, and you've been there a year.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Are you forgotten then by who ever decides assignments?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: No, see I had my order was to be released from active duty.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: No, I mean had you not.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Oh, I see.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: First of all, how does an officer get moved from for example from the Naval Academy to Japan and then how to you leave there? Do they, does your number come up or how does that work?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, each year when we fill out a fitness report which was standard for everybody, you could put down your choice as far as your next duty station. So, I never got mine. Some detail officer in the Navy Department in Washington assigns people and they try to assign you to different ships, different stations. Normally, the first seven years are all sea duty attached to a ship. My one year at the Naval Academy was an exception because of the superintendent's experiment. So, if I had not resigned I would have been on that minesweeper about two years and then I would have been assigned to --

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Then you would have been moved?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I would have been moved.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: You would not have been on the mine sweeper for the rest of your career?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Oh, no. The normal tour was 18 to 24 months.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see. So you --

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Because it was, it wasn't. Well, I guess it was considered hazardous duty.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: The only real hazardous duty were aviation and submarines. They got extra pay in those days; 10% in pay. That's why so many people liked that. As a matter of fact when I graduated, my monthly pay was 180 dollars a month which to me was great because I didn't have any money up to then. But we, at that time we got the 10 percent sea pay, another 18 dollars a month that was nice.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I'll bet.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: But then after the, oh, maybe six months later, the sea pay was eliminated. So, I'm back to 180 a month.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, according to the notes we have made, your first service dates were 6/44 to 7/50?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And then a little over a year later you're back in the Service and it appears that it was during the Korean War?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, were you called to active duty or did you ask for active duty again?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, I figured that because the Korean War was on that sooner or later they were going to recall people to active duty and in the meantime I got a job with Owens Illinois I was working, I worked for two months at a plant in Illinois and then another plant in New Jersey, and I went back to Illinois and I came home from work one day and I had a big brown envelope -- Orders for two years active duty. They gave me about two weeks to report.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, this was the government's determination?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Oh, yes, someone had gone through the record, back in those days used those IBM cards, and someone went through the record, they pushed the button and they said, we need people to serve as instructors at the officer candidate school and we're starting in Newport, Rhode Island and my name fell out because I had one year as an instructor at the Naval Academy teaching navigation. So, I was ordered back there to teach.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Now, you have a job you said at Owenville, Illinois?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And now you're called to active duty?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Was it a requirement that Owens Illinois hold a job or an opening for you when you returned?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes, and they did.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, then you spent two years as an instructor at Newport, Rhode Island in Officers Candidate School?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: But then as I look at the record I see a year after, in 10/54 you are now in the Reserves?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: No, actually I was in the Reserve from 1950 on. During the time I was on actively duty from '51 to '53 I was not a regular major, I was a reserve officer.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, then when you were recalled in October of '51 you are a reservist at that time?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes, I was. When I resigned my regular Navy commission, I had to agree to serve in the living reserve for the will and pleasure of the president.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And his pleasure was that you would be recalled?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: The pleasure was I was being recalled. I was needed, super, so I shortly after I finished two years at Newport, I was working in a plant in New Jersey for Owenville Mine. They were very good about that. I got credit for those two years. I worked for Owensville, Illinois for 30 years but I had two years of military leave of absence so I got credited for 32 years of service. So, I thought, well, if they're going to keep calling me back I better join a unit, so I did in Camden, New Jersey, and I drove there weekly and I took two week training duty every year until 1960 when he moved to Toledo. I did the same thing here from 1960 to 1974, I was in the Active Reserve. I went to sometimes weekend drills, sometimes one night a week but always at least two weeks training duty every year. I used to alternate, go to sea duty one year and training school the next year.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: But you were not called to active duty after October of '52?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: That's correct. I had mobilization orders.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, you could have?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yeah, I could have. I had mobilization orders in my pocket literally for 22 years and I was not recalled during the Viet Nam or later.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Here are just a sample of some of the ships I was on on my two weeks training duties. I was on an aircraft carrier, heavy cruiser, a light cruiser, a destroyer, Destroyer SGood, Destroyer Tender, LST, which is landship ship tank, LCI which is landing craft infantry, and a diesel submarine. Then some of the short duties I had and I had to apply for all of these, I attended the Senior Reserve Officer course at the Naval War College in Newport, Rhode Island. I'm a graduate of that. I also graduated from the National War College in Washington, D.C. I attended an Industrial Relations seminar in New Orleans which was also Mardi Gras time which was nice. I was on the staff of the Commander of the Sixth Fleet on a heavy cruiser. I spent two years, two summers, at the Navy Department in Washington, D.C. in the Office of Naval Materiel where I learned some things the Navy was doing to the submarines that I was able to apply to my work with Owens Illinois. I went through inspector training school in Philadelphia which is near where I live, and I went to an administration seminar in Philadelphia and I went to an ABC Warfare School in Philadelphia. that's the Thomas Biological and Chemical Warfare, so those are all very interesting things.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Let's move forward a little bit. You went to work or you were working for Owens Illinois?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And you worked there how many years?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Thirty-two years.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: But that was not the end of your career. What did you do after that?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, I still worked for 0I and after I finished my reserve duty, after a total of 30 years, I told my wife, you know, I've been spending a lot of time with the Reserve, what can I do to utilize that time with them. She says, why don't you go to get a master's degree that you often talked about, and I said okay, I was thinking the same thing. So, I enrolled at the University of Toledo in the College of Business Administration and while I was still working full time and traveling, I can't believe I earned a Master's Degree in business administration. Then I decided that one day I wanted to be on the faculty, so I went another five years and got a Doctorate. Then after I got my Doctorate, I was still working for OI, I taught school in the College of Business for three years part-time, this one course. Finally, the chairman of the department said, why don't you retire from OI and come over here full time. He said, I can give you a senior faculty position, so I thought about it and I said I will, I will do it. So, I retired from OI after 33 years, went on the, that was in September of 1982. I joined the faculty the next day and was full time for almost 20 years, and got tenure after six years and as I mentioned earlier, I taught all the courses that I used to do full time at OI which the students seemed to really like. In fact, I had one fellow in one of my classes who was a superintendent at the Ford Plant in Flat Rock, near there, along I-75, you used to see it every day.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Woodhaven.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Yeah, that's the one, Woodhaven Camping Ground, and after about two or three weeks in class he came up to me, he said Dr. Clegg, you're the first professor I've had at the university who knew what the hell he was talking about, which I thought was nice. He was a really good student and he later went on and got an MBA.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I have no comment. I'm a neutral person, an interviewer. So, you have had quite a career?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Well, yes. I decided that I would stay at the University of Toledo well past 65 because I was enjoying it. My son used to say, Dad, why don't you retire, you're old enough, and I said, Bill, I said, this is my hobby and they're paying me to do it. Why would I want to retire, but after a while I knew I probably couldn't work too much longer, and about the same time the university offered an early incentive plan for people to retire and they said we'll give you one year for every five up to a maximum of three years, well, I had almost 20 years full times, and I brought in five years military that increased my UP Service, so they said we'll give you three more years, so I took it, and at the age of 74, I took my early incentive retirement plan and retired and I did a little consulting work after that, but I'm fully retired now.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, your employment is done now but I understand also that you are very active in the Retired Officers Association. Yes, I joined the Military Officers, it used to be called the TROA, The Retired Officers Association which changed about a year ago to MOAA which is Military Officers Association of America. I joined that and I attend meetings when I'm able. I also joined the American Legion after I retired from the university. I'm not a regular attendor, they meet every Friday. We're doing a lot of weekends visiting grandchildren and take a hike and we travel a little bit. So, I don't attend as many meetings as I would like and then about two years ago I joined the Navy League what is a very active organization, very nice organization. I'm also a life member of the Naval Academy Alumni Association and that meets once a month at the DIO (ph) Club and I'm also a life member of the Legal Alumni Association, so I don't think I'm joining any more clubs and in between my wife and I play duplicate bridge a lot and we travel around Ohio and Michigan playing in duplicate bridge tournaments. That's usually over a weekend too.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: I see, I see. So yours has been a full life.

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I think so. When you talk with my wife, find that hers is even more interesting.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: In the military for you was a very positive experience?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: Oh, yes, we've often said that we wish that our two children had had the opportunity to serve in the military. Any one would benefit. You know, there are hard times and many people go on dangerous assignments and a lot of people severely wounded and gave their final, but still after it all I wouldn't have missed it for the -- I wouldn't have missed those 22 years in the active reserve because the one thing that gave me a chance to maintain my target in North Korea, I was promoted in those years up to the rank as a Major Captain and I had some pretty responsible assignments. I started out as a training officer and then a group supervisory officer and then an executive officer and then I commanded my own unit here in Toledo for three years, and then I went on the group commander staff, that's where Jeff and Jim Gilbert was the group commander. I was his chief staff officer for five years and when he finished his to tour I later became group commander. I had ten units in northwestern Ohio under my command and that was a massive tour of three years and when I came back I still stayed in the Active Reserve with a number of other units until I finished my total of 30 years and then I retired in 1974.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: So, if a young man came to you today and said I'm considering a military career?

sp.speaker: William Clegg
sp.p: I wouldn't hesitate to recommend. I do a lot of interviewing. When I was at the university I interviewed prospective candidates for the Reserve Officer Training Program and I would say the same thing to them. I interviewed people who wanted to go to the Naval Academy and encouraged them. I've written letters on their behalf to see if they can get an appointment. If not every congressman or senator uses civil service exams. Some of them are recommendations from committees, we have a group here in Toledo called Blue and Gold Officers based on the Navy colors. They interview candidates and recommend who they have seen and if they're fortunate enough may get an appointment. They still have to qualify. Getting an appointment is the first step. You still have to qualify either by taking the admissions test or if you have had college and you get good enough grades, you can use those to substantiate your qualifications and then you have to pass a very rigid physical. I couldn't pass a physical today because of my eyes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Well, you have given well to your country.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: The country has responded. William Legg: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: And this has been a very good interview because you are so positive about your military experience. William Legg: Well, again, I would never hesitate to do the same thing again. If I could have passed the physical qualifications early on, who knows I might have gone into aviation or submarines or who knows, but I couldn't do either one.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: This seems an appropriate time then to end our interview. William Legg: Well, thank you very much. I really enjoyed it.

sp.speaker: Andrew Fisher
sp.p: Thank you. (Interview concluded)
